claims.text: CoCo Ichibanya's standard curry sauce/roux is wheat-based, so the regular curry is NOT gluten-free or celiac-safe. The chain does offer a separate sealed/retort low-allergen curry made without designated allergens, which is the only gluten-conscious option; confirm with staff that it is the one being served and ask how it is heated and plated to avoid contact with the standard roux.

This is a shared kitchen serving primarily wheat-based curry, plus fried items and curry ramen (wheat noodles). For a strict celiac, cross-contact risk from the standard roux, shared utensils, and fryers should be assumed unless staff confirm otherwise.

CoCo Ichibanya offers vegetarian/vegan-leaning curry options at some locations, but they are prepared in a kitchen that also handles meat, dairy and egg toppings. Vegan diners should confirm the specific curry base is plant-based and ask about shared cooking surfaces and utensils.
The chain publishes allergen information and offers a dedicated low-allergen (allergen-free) curry product, which is more than many independent curry shops provide.

No specific gluten-free or cross-contamination information is documented. The kitchen is a one-person operation cooking many dishes from scratch in a small space, so shared equipment is likely; celiac diners should confirm directly before relying on any dish.
Several menu items are wheat-based or fried (falafel balls, fried tempeh and vegetables, noodle dishes), so a strictly gluten-free meal is not something the sources confirm.

No information is available on whether the soy sauce or seasonings used are wheat-free. As with most Japanese kitchens, standard soy sauce typically contains wheat; ask the owner about specific sauces if you are celiac.

Despite an existing note of 'fully vegan,' sources indicate PELGAG is a mixed menu: it serves non-vegan items (including meat) alongside clearly labeled vegan options, all prepared in the same small one-person kitchen. Vegan dishes are available but shared prep means some cross-contact is possible.
Vegan options are clearly marked on the menu (an English menu is available), so you can identify plant-based dishes, but the venue is not an all-vegan kitchen.
The listing advises guests to tell staff about vegetarian/vegan needs and any allergies when choosing a dish, suggesting the owner will accommodate on request.
Reviewers describe the owner as friendly and hands-on, but there are no specific reports about formal allergy protocols.
Vegan dishes are clearly labeled and an English menu is available, making it easy to identify plant-based options.
The owner cooks everything from scratch and is approachable, so questions about ingredients can be raised directly.
The staff invite diners to share vegan and allergy needs before ordering so a suitable dish can be chosen.

The restaurant markets itself as offering Halal, Vegan and Gluten-Free options, but no published source describes how gluten-free items are kept separate from wheat-based ones (buns, ramen noodles, sauces) during prep. A celiac diner should confirm dedicated handling with staff before ordering.

The menu includes a shared French fries item served alongside burgers; whether fries share a fryer with any battered or breaded item is not documented, so cross-contact in the fryer cannot be ruled out.

Burgers are served with a house 'sauce' and the menu also features ramen; the specific ingredients of these sauces and broths are not published. As most Japanese soy sauce and many Japanese sauces contain wheat, anyone strictly avoiding gluten should verify each sauce and the ramen broth/noodles directly with the restaurant.

This is fundamentally a Wagyu beef restaurant (steak, Wagyu burgers, ramen) that advertises a vegan option. Any vegan dish would be prepared in a kitchen that primarily handles beef, so shared grills, utensils and surfaces are a realistic cross-contact concern; confirm separate preparation with staff if strict.

For allergen questions the restaurant directs guests to phone the store directly rather than relying on the online listing, indicating allergen details are handled case by case with staff (store phone listed on its delivery page).
The restaurant explicitly advertises Halal, Vegan and Gluten-Free options, so accommodating these diets is part of its stated offering - a good starting point for a conversation with staff.
As an alcohol-free, Muslim-friendly venue that hand-selects halal-certified Wagyu, the kitchen is already used to sourcing-conscious, restriction-aware service.

CoCo Ichibanya's standard curry roux contains wheat, so the regular menu is not gluten-free. The chain's dedicated low-allergen curry is the route for celiac and GF diners — confirm with staff that you are being served the allergen-free product, not the standard sauce.
Rice and other menu items are prepped in a shared kitchen that also handles wheat, so cross-contact on rice and shared surfaces is possible even when ordering the allergen-free curry.
The standard curry and many toppings can contain soybean and wheat. As with most Japanese kitchens, soy-based seasonings here are likely to contain wheat — not safe to assume otherwise.

Vegetarian and vegan curry options exist within the CoCo Ichibanya brand, but they are prepared in a kitchen that also handles meat, dairy, egg and fish, so cross-contact is possible. Vegans avoiding trace animal contact should ask staff how the vegetarian curry is prepared and served.

The chain publishes allergen information and offers a dedicated allergen-free (low-allergen) curry, which signals a company-wide awareness of allergies; ask staff for the allergen sheet (an English QR-code version is available) before ordering.

CoCo Ichibanya offers a dedicated allergen-free curry that is free of wheat, dairy, egg, buckwheat, crab and shrimp — including a children's version — which is unusually accommodating for a Japanese curry chain and a genuine option for wheat-avoiding and celiac diners (served as a separate, pre-prepared product).
An allergen information sheet is available, with an English version accessible by QR code, so you can check ingredients per item before ordering.
Curry is made to order with adjustable toppings, spice and rice, making it easier to leave out specific ingredients you need to avoid.

The entire menu is gluten-free because the owner is gluten-intolerant herself, which removes wheat-flour from the core of the kitchen and is the biggest single point in the cafe's favor for GF diners.

Sources disagree on how strictly cross-contamination is controlled: one gluten-free directory lists it as celiac-friendly with dedicated appliances, while another states plainly it is NOT a dedicated gluten-free facility and may not be safe for celiac disease. Celiac diners should confirm preparation directly with the owner.

At least one reviewer warns that the bento box is not safe for celiacs because it contains soy sauce — a reminder that standard Japanese soy sauce typically contains wheat. Ask which items use soy sauce before ordering.

There are dedicated vegan options, notably a vegan chickpea curry, and reviewers mention plenty of vegan items; no specific reports were found on vegan cross-contact in a kitchen that also handles dairy cakes and cheese, so vegan diners should confirm shared-equipment handling with the owner.

The cafe is run by a single owner who is gluten-intolerant herself and is described as kind and helpful, which makes direct conversation about your needs straightforward — but it also means there is no separate trained allergy team, so clear, item-by-item questions are worthwhile.
Everything on the menu is gluten-free, made from scratch by an owner who shares the intolerance — rare and reassuring for GF diners.

Homemade chiffon and rice-flour cakes are widely praised as light and fluffy, and many diners report the rice-flour pizza impressed even gluten-eaters; a vegan chickpea curry is available for plant-based guests.

The allergen-free curry is a fully cooked retort product: it arrives in a sealed, factory-prepared heated pouch opened at the table, so the curry sauce itself never touches the regular kitchen line. This sealed-pouch service is the main reason gluten-free diners report it dependable.
The principal remaining cross-contact point is the rice, cooked in a shared rice cooker used for all orders. Very sensitive diners may want to ask about this or skip the rice.
The allergen-free curry is documented as free of wheat, dairy, egg, buckwheat, crab and shrimp.

No soy sauce concern surfaced for the allergen-free curry, which is wheat-free by formulation. The regular menu curry sauces are a different matter and are not wheat-safe, so order specifically from the allergen-free option rather than a standard curry.

A meat-free 'vegetarian curry' sauce is offered (no animal meat, fish, shellfish, egg, dairy or honey), but it shares a production line with dairy, so trace dairy is possible. Strict vegans should be aware of this.

The standard curry sauce is NOT vegan or vegetarian (contains meat, fish extract, milk, cheese and honey). Always order from the marked vegetarian section rather than assuming a plain curry is meat-free.
Watch out for non-vegan items that look plant-based: keema sauce contains chicken and the udon soup contains fish extract.

The chain publishes a full allergen matrix and store menus carry detailed allergen descriptions, and travelers report staff being helpful in flagging which sides can be prepared safely when you state your dietary need at ordering.
A sealed, pre-packaged allergen-free curry that is opened at the table is unusually reassuring for celiac and multi-allergy diners, and it is inexpensive and widely available.
Beyond gluten-free, a clearly marked meat-free curry exists, so the same restaurant can serve both gluten-free and vegetarian/vegan diners in one stop.

This is a wheat-aware caution, not a celiac-safe rating. The menu includes gyoza (wheat-flour wrappers), soy-meat skewers (commonly seasoned with soy sauce and may be wheat-based), and deep-fried tofu in the obanzai assortment, so wheat and shared frying/cooking surfaces are present. No source documents gluten-free preparation, a dedicated fryer, or celiac protocols. Treat as not celiac-safe unless you confirm specific dishes and handling directly with the cooks.
The obanzai assortment is described as including deep-fried tofu, indicating frying happens in the kitchen; no information confirms whether the fryer is dedicated or gluten-free.

The gyoza are served with house-made soy sauce, and soy-meat skewers are part of the menu. Most Japanese soy sauce is brewed with wheat, and no source states this soy sauce or seasoning is wheat-free. Assume it contains gluten unless the cooks confirm otherwise.

Nijiya is a fully vegan kitchen with no animal products on the premises, so the risk of animal-product cross-contact is effectively nil. The dashi is built from konbu, dried shiitake, daikon and burdock rather than fish, so it is plant-based.
A reviewer reported the staff have good English and are very attentive, and will be accommodating with sensitivities such as garlic and spices.
With only the two owner-cooks running a six-to-seven-seat counter, requests can be discussed directly, though the very small kitchen may limit how strictly cross-contamination can be controlled.
Entirely vegan menu with a plant-based dashi (konbu, dried shiitake, daikon, burdock) instead of fish stock, so no hidden animal products.
Gyoza are made without leek, shallot or garlic, which helps diners avoiding alliums.
Attentive, English-speaking staff described as accommodating to sensitivities like garlic and spices.

This is a fully vegan macrobiotic kitchen built around whole grains and vegetables, and it is reported to offer a gluten-free option, with some diners describing a gluten-free set lunch that the kitchen can prepare if given advance notice. However, no source documents a dedicated gluten-free preparation area or specific cross-contamination protocols, so celiac diners should confirm directly before ordering.

The kitchen is noted for using traditionally made soy sauce. Most traditional Japanese soy sauce is brewed with wheat, so unless a wheat-free tamari is confirmed, the soy sauce here should be assumed to contain wheat. Celiac diners should ask specifically whether a gluten-free soy sauce or tamari is used in their dish.

The food is vegan and macrobiotic. One note flags that a single item on the broader menu may contain cheese, so vegans should confirm their specific dish (the bento boxes are the plant-based mainstay).
English-speaking staff will explain the ingredients used and their health benefits, and the kitchen can make most things on the menu allium-free (no garlic/onion).
Staff are described as welcoming questions about the food, and have accommodated strict requests such as Jain dietary needs.
Fully vegan macrobiotic menu with detailed ingredient and nutrition information provided in multiple languages, making it easy to see what is in each dish.
A gluten-free option is reported to be available, and the kitchen is willing to prepare a gluten-free set lunch with advance notice.
Most menu items can be made allium-free on request, and staff have a track record of handling restrictive diets thoughtfully.
